- Pass the stride as runtime `tl.int32` state through both gfx950 Gluon KV loaders.
- Keep the allocated-once KV-cache layout strides as `constexpr`.
- Keep the diff code-only, without adding to CI runtime.

## Root cause

SGLang serving can produce padded block tables with different row strides across batches. The gfx950 Gluon kernel stored `block_table_stride` in `AttentionConfig`, making every new stride part of the JIT compile key.

A matched serving profile observed seven Gluon compilations inside the measured request, adding 5.75 seconds of gaps immediately before unified-attention launches even though the compiled Gluon kernels themselves were faster than the Triton kernels.

The stride is bounded by the per-request block-table width, so runtime `tl.int32` is sufficient. `AsyncKVLoader` and `AsyncGatherKVLoader` now receive it as runtime state. The gather loader explicitly narrows its clamped block-table indices to `gl.int32`, as required by the CDNA buffer-load interface.

## Validation

### Changing-stride probe

The same logical page table was invoked with seven padded strides from 60000 through 60511.

| Measurement | Compile-time stride | Runtime `tl.int32` stride |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cold total | 5,858.85 ms | 2,371.42 ms |
| Cached total | 330.66 ms | 332.07 ms |
| Compile-like cold calls | 7 | 2 |
| Finite-output failures | 0 | 0 |
| Maximum output difference | — | `6.11e-5` |

The initial variants are bounded; subsequent changing stride values no longer create a new binary.

### Loader coverage

External focused validation exercised changing padded widths through:

- `AsyncGatherKVLoader` with block size 1.
- `AsyncKVLoader` with block size 64.

Both paths remained finite and produced identical outputs across the tested widths.

### Matched serving profile

The same 60K-input, 128-output, concurrency-4 profile was run before and after the change.

| Metric | Compile-time stride | Runtime `tl.int32` stride |
|---|---:|---:|
| Successful requests | 8/8 | 8/8 |
| Benchmark duration | 130.37 s | 108.31 s |
| Input throughput | 3,681.93 tok/s | 4,431.69 tok/s |
| Output throughput | 7.85 tok/s | 9.45 tok/s |
| Main-run Gluon compilations | 7 | 0 |
| Prefill gaps | 5,724.51 ms | 31.22 ms |
| Decode gaps | 8.08 ms | 8.04 ms |

This is a 20.4% input-throughput recovery and a 16.9% duration reduction, with no main-run compilation left in the trace.

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 -m py_compile aiter/ops/triton/_gluon_kernels/gfx950/attention/unified_attention.py`
- [x] Ruff check and format check.
- [x] Seven-width compile/cache probe.
- [x] Direct and gather KV-loader output comparison.
- [x] Matched serving profile with trace inspection.
- [ ] Upstream CI.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Add gluon support for MXFP4 and MXFP8 quant kernel in gfx1250
[HIP] [Bugfix] paged_attention_ragged: scale FP8 softmax probabilities into the e4m3 normal range
body:
## Summary

On the FP8 KV-cache path, `paged_attention_ragged` normalizes the softmax
probabilities to sum = 1 within a partition and *then* casts them to
`fp8_e4m3` for the PV MFMA. With the default `partition_size = 256` and a
typical near-uniform attention distribution, every probability lands at ≈2⁻⁸ —
**subnormal in e4m3** (min normal 2⁻⁶, subnormal step 2⁻⁹), where the relative
ulp is ½. The result is ~15% RMS error on `P`, which propagates 1:1 to the
attention output.

The BF16 path does not have this problem, and **aiter's own Gluon paged-decode
kernel already implements the fix**.

## Reproduction

aiter's only FP8-KV test for this op fails on a stock image:

```console
$ python3 -m pytest op_tests/test_pa_ragged.py -k fp8_kv_nhd -x -q
FAILED op_tests/test_pa_ragged.py::test_paged_attention_ragged_glm_gqa_fp8_kv_nhd
1 failed, 13824 deselected, 2 warnings in 19.52s

Greatest relative difference: 0.355 (up to 0.03 allowed)
```

Environment: MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.0, torch 2.9.0a0, image
`lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910` + aiter
`4ad99832823dde2315b361cbd3b54b1c5c12acd5`.

That test uses head_size 128, 8 KV heads, seq_len **128** — a single partition —
and it *barely* fails (3 of 24576 elements). At realistic decode contexts the
mechanism is pervasive. Measured against an fp32 PyTorch reference at
head_dim 256, 1 KV head, 4 query heads, context 8192 (32 partitions):

| KV cache | `kv_cache_dtype` | mean relative error |
|---|---|---|
| bf16 | `"auto"` | **0.0032** |
| fp8_e4m3fn | `"fp8_e4m3"` | **0.1422** |

Error is flat in context length (0.140 / 0.147 / 0.149 at ctx 256 / 1024 / 4096)
— consistent with per-token independent rounding rather than an accumulation
problem — and identical for `"NHD"` and `"HND"`, so it is not a layout issue.

## Root cause

`csrc/cpp_itfs/pa/pa_kernels.cuh`:

* **`:586-588`** — `inv_sum_scale = 1/(partition_exp_sum + 1e-6) * exp(warp_max - partition_max)`.
  `P` is fully normalized to sum 1.
* **`:633-647`** — `d_out *= inv_sum_scale`, then
  `__builtin_amdgcn_cvt_pk_fp8_f32(...)`. The **already-normalized** `P` is cast
  to e4m3.
* **`:794`** — `gcn_mfma16x16x32_instr<__hip_fp8_e4m3, ...>` consumes it.
* **`:596-621`** — the `kAuto`/bf16 branch keeps `P` in bf16, which represents
  2⁻⁸ exactly. Hence the 0.3% agreement there.

`Q` is also cast to fp8 on this path (`:379-409`), contributing a further ~0.7%.

At `partition_size = 256`, **100% of P values measured fall in the e4m3
subnormal range**, with RMS relative rounding error 0.163 — matching the observed
0.153. Raising `partition_size` to 512 (p ≈ 2⁻⁹) drives the error to **1.04**,
which is the predicted behaviour if this diagnosis is right.

### Attribution, by emulation

A partition-aware fp32 model with each rounding step toggled independently
(ctx 2048, partition 256; shipped kernel vs exact = 0.1534):

| emulated model | kernel-vs-model | model-vs-exact |
|---|---|---|
| exact fp32 | 0.1534 | 0.0000 |
| + bf16 partial writeback | 0.1534 | 0.0017 |
| + fp8 Q only | 0.1528 | 0.0070 |
| + fp8 P only | 0.0468 | 0.1523 |
| **+ fp8 Q and fp8 P** | **0.0014** | **0.1534** |

Adding only the two fp8 casts reproduces the shipped kernel to 0.14%.

## Fix (implemented and validated)

Normalize `P` by the partition **max** rather than the sum — putting the largest
value inside the e4m3 normal range — and fold `1/exp_sum` into the fp32 output
after the MFMA. Same instruction count, same MFMA, no extra memory traffic.

`upstream/aiter-pa-ragged-fp8-fix.patch` (54 insertions in `pa_kernels.cuh`)
splits `inv_sum_scale` into a pre-cast and a post-MFMA factor inside the existing
`if constexpr(KV_DTYPE != kAuto)` branches, so the BF16 path is untouched. The
scale is the largest **power of two** inside the normal range (256 on gfx950,
128 on gfx942 where e4m3 is fnuz) rather than the range maximum: a power of two
is exact in binary, so the rescale introduces no rounding of its own and cannot
push the cast into saturation. The two factors multiply back to `inv_sum_scale`
exactly, so the result is unchanged in exact arithmetic — only the rounding
improves.

Only `_paged_attention_kernel` needs it. `_paged_attention_kernel_EXPERIMENTAL`
shares the pattern but is bf16-only (`pa_ragged.py:32` requires
`kv_dtype == "__hip_bfloat16"`), so it never reaches the fp8 branch.

### Validation

MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.0, same container before and after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `test_paged_attention_ragged_glm_gqa_fp8_kv_nhd` | **FAIL** (rel diff 0.355 vs 0.03) | **PASS** |
| fp8 error vs fp32 reference, bs 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 | 0.1417 / 0.1432 / 0.1420 / 0.1426 | **0.0273 / 0.0277 / 0.0276 / 0.0276** |
| bf16 error, same shapes | 0.00317 / 0.00325 / 0.00322 / 0.00319 | 0.00317 / 0.00325 / 0.00322 / 0.00319 |
| bf16 output checksum | 0.037695 / 0.706248 / 0.237597 / −1.877981 | **bit-identical** |
| fp8 kernel time (µs) | 13.49 / 14.57 / 35.36 / 59.68 | 13.51 / 14.58 / 35.65 / 59.50 |
| bf16 kernel time (µs) | 14.82 / 20.21 / 62.96 / 137.99 | 14.82 / 20.26 / 62.82 / 138.03 |

**5.2× error reduction, timing neutral to within noise, BF16 bit-identical.**
Broader regression: 192 passed / 0 failed on a BF16 slice of
`test_pa_ragged.py`. Harness: `notes/pa_fix_validate.py`.

The residual 0.0277 is expected and is not this defect — the KV cache is
genuinely fp8, and Q is also cast to fp8 for the QK MFMA (`:379-409`), which the
emulation attributed ~0.007 to. Both are deliberate design choices, unlike the
subnormal P.

This is what aiter's own Gluon kernel does, so the approach is already
established in-tree —
`aiter/ops/triton/gluon/pa_decode_gluon.py`:

* **`:918`** keeps `attention_probs = exp2(qk - max)` unnormalized
* **`:943`** multiplies by `FP8_MAX_VALUE` (448) before the cast, with a
  compensating `probability_scale` at **`:944` / `:975`**
* **`:990`** applies `1/exp_sums` only after the MFMA
* **`:933`**, in as many words: *"Scale the maximum value of value_scale to
  FP8_MAX_VALUE to improve the precision of P * V."*

## Test coverage gap

`op_tests/test_pa_ragged.py:686-688` — the main parametrized `test_paged_attention`
**skips every quantized-cache case** for the `Shomy` variant, so
`paged_attention_ragged` has no FP8-KV coverage in the main matrix. The single
dedicated test at `:452-514` uses `rtol = atol = 3e-2`, head_size 128, seq_len
128, and never exercises a multi-partition context or head_dim 256.

Suggest extending it to cover multi-partition contexts (≥ 1024 tokens) and
head_dim 256, which is where the defect is largest.

## Impact

`paged_attention_ragged` is the decode attention op SGLang's aiter backend calls
for non-MLA models on ROCm
(`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/aiter_backend.py:3312`), and
`--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` is a common production setting. Any deployment
combining the two is running decode attention with ~15% error on the attention
probabilities.

I have not measured downstream task-accuracy impact — softmax outputs are
averages over many values and the error is zero-mean, so end-to-end damage may
be much smaller than the per-tensor number suggests. The kernel-level error is
nonetheless far outside the op's own stated tolerance.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Fused Qwen3-Next GDN decode op for gfx950
body:
# [Triton/Gluon] Fused Qwen3-Next GDN decode op for gfx950

## Motivation

Qwen3-Next's Gated DeltaNet decode step runs as four separate kernels today:

```
fused_qkvzba_split_reshape_cat  ->  causal_conv1d_update
  ->  fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode  ->  gated RMSNorm
```

aiter has all the pieces for GDN — `chunk_gated_delta_rule`,
`fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule`, `causal_conv1d_update_split_qkv`,
`gated_rmsnorm_fp8_group_quant` — but **not the single-launch fusion**, and not
one that consumes the packed `qkvz`/`ba` projections directly.

This adds that op. On 4x MI355X / TP4 with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 it is
worth **+6.0% to +9.1% end-to-end output throughput** when wired into SGLang
(companion PR), with no accuracy regression.

### Why a new op rather than a mode on `fused_kda_decode`

`fused_kda_decode` is the same *shape* of fusion — conv, recurrence, gated norm,
one launch — but it implements **KDA**, and the differences are structural, not
parametric:

| | `fused_kda_decode` | this op |
|---|---|---|
| head topology | one `H`; q/k/v all `H` heads | `VH == 2*KH` |
| gate | `lower_bound * sigmoid(exp(A)*(a+dt))`, vector over K | `exp(-exp(A_log)*softplus(a+dt))`, scalar per head |
| output gate | `sigmoid(z)` | `z * sigmoid(z)` (SiLU) |
| conv bias | none | seeds the accumulator |
| input | pre-split `mixed_qkv`/`gate`/`beta` | packed `qkvz`/`ba`, split internally |

The head topology alone settles it: KDA's `lp = H*K`, `q_off = i_h*K`,
`v_off = 2*lp + i_h*V` offsets cannot express `VH = 2*KH`. A mode flag would
double an existing kernel's branch factor to host a different algorithm, so this
ships as a sibling instead. `fused_kda_decode` is not exported from
`gated_delta_net/__init__.py`, so no existing interface is perturbed.

## Modifications

New:
  * `aiter/ops/triton/_gluon_kernels/gfx950/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`                            
    — the Gluon kernels. Two decompositions behind one entry point:                                              
    * **batch < 128** — `_fused_decode` / `_fused_decode_tiled`. One eight-wave                                  
      workgroup owns a token/key-head group's convolution history and both FP32                                  
      value-head states, with prefetch and tiling to hide memory latency while                                   
      the machine is under-occupied.                                                                             
    * **batch >= 128** — `_decode_group`, which keeps the whole `[V, K]` state                                   
      tile in registers across both matrix-vector products. Above that threshold                                 
      the kernel is bandwidth-bound, where the latency-hiding machinery stops                                    
      paying and the simpler traffic pattern reaches a better fraction of peak.                                  
                                                                                                                 
    Selection is a **range check, not a shape table**, so every batch size is                                    
    covered.  
* `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — public wrapper,
  shape/dtype validation and the support predicate.
* `op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — a pure-torch fp32
  reference plus correctness, pad-slot, bf16-only and determinism tests.
* `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — bandwidth and
  roofline sweep.

Modified:
* `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/__init__.py` — export the op and its
  predicate.

### What it fuses

1. unpack packed `projected_qkvz` -> Q/K/V/Z and `projected_ba` -> b/a
2. depthwise causal conv1d against the rolling window, **with bias**, + SiLU
3. delta-rule gating, `decay = exp(-exp(A_log) * softplus(a + dt_bias))`
4. FP32 recurrent state update at `ssm_state[indices]`
5. gated RMSNorm with a SiLU gate
6. *optional* per-head group-128 FP8 quantization

Stage 6 is opt-in via `quant_dtype=`. With `None` the op returns bf16 only,
because an unquantized `Linear` consumer cannot accept an `(fp8, scales)` tuple.

### `pad_slot_id`

Rows whose state index equals `pad_slot_id` (default `-1`) are skipped without
reading or writing state. This matches what the other indexed-state ops in this
directory already do — `fused_conv_recurrent_norm` returns on `state_idx < 0`,
`causal_conv1d_update_split_qkv` takes an explicit `pad_slot_id` — and it is the
contract SGLang's `replay_state_indices_validator` documents. Measured cost:
**0.2-0.3%**, i.e. within noise.

## Scope and supported shapes

Deliberately narrow, and **reported rather than asserted**:
`fused_gdn_decode_qkvz_supported()` returns `(bool, reason)` so callers fall
back and can log why.

* gfx950 only — CDNA buffer addressing, `v_exp_f32`/`v_rcp_f32` inline asm,
  explicit register layouts
* `num_v_heads == 2 * num_k_heads`; `head_k_dim == head_v_dim == 128`
* conv width 4; contiguous conv and recurrent state pools
* bf16 packed projections / conv weight / conv bias / `dt_bias` / `norm_weight`;
  fp32 `A_log` and `ssm_state`; int32 state indices
* fp8 output, when requested, is `e4m3fn` or `e4m3fnuz`

**No CUDA path is affected.** The op is reachable only through its own module,
and every caller is expected to gate on the predicate.

## Accuracy Tests

`pytest op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — **22 passed** on
MI355X / ROCm 7.0 / Triton 3.8.

* `test_fused_gdn_decode_correctness` at batch 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 —
  output, scales, and both mutated state pools against the fp32 reference at
  ATOL/RTOL 0.05, the bar this directory already uses for `fused_kda_decode`.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_pad_slot` — `PAD_SLOT_ID` rows leave `ssm_state` and
  `conv_state` bit-unchanged.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_bf16_only` — `quant_dtype=None` returns `(out, None, None)`.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_determinism` — same inputs twice, bit-identical.
* Eleven reference-only tests pin the packed layout, gate algebra and quant
  round-trip independently of the kernel.

The reference itself was validated before being trusted: run against **seven
independent implementations of this kernel across nine batch sizes**, it agrees
on every one, and `conv_state` matches **bit-exactly** on all 63 combinations.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Hardware: 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950), TP4 / EP1.
Image: `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910` (ROCm 7.0,
Triton 3.8.0, torch 2.9). Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8`.

### Kernel level

Per-launch time under **CUDA graph replay** with a fixed 512-slot state pool.
Both matter: timing the Python call instead of the kernel produces a flat ~25 us
floor that is host overhead, and sizing the pool to the batch puts small batches
entirely in cache.

  | batch | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 192 | 256 |                                                     
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|                                                                  
  | this op (us/call) | 9.70 | 9.73 | 9.80 | 10.02 | 9.84 | 10.40 | 14.24 | 26.95 | 36.81 | 46.52 | 

Replaced chain, same conditions, per decode step over 36 GDN layers:
**830.8 us -> 279.2 us (2.98x)** for the four kernels listed in Motivation.

### Roofline

`python3 op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`, MI355X
(8.0 TB/s peak HBM). The op performs no MFMA and no `gl.dot`; it is bound by the
FP32 recurrent state, read and written once per token per value head, which
dominates every other tensor by an order of magnitude.

  | batch | 1 | 8 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 192 | 256 |                                                                  
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|                                                                              
  | us/call | 9.39 | 9.69 | 10.40 | 14.24 | 26.95 | 36.81 | 46.52 |                                              
  | TB/s | 0.12 | 0.89 | 3.33 | 4.87 | 5.14 | 5.65 | **5.96** |
  | % peak | 1.4% | 11.2% | 41.6% | 60.8% | 64.3% | 70.6% | **74.5%** |

  Two regimes, and they are why the op carries two decompositions. Up to batch
  ~32 it is **latency-bound** — there is not enough state traffic to fill the
  machine, and time is nearly flat at ~9.4-10.4 us regardless of batch, so
  prefetch and tiling pay. From batch 64 it becomes **bandwidth-bound**, where
  that machinery stops paying and the register-resident tile reaches a better
  fraction of peak: **74.5% at batch 256**.

  A single decomposition plateaued at 5.20 TB/s (65%) there. Three candidate fixes
  were tested and rejected before concluding the gap was structural: extra HBM
  passes (identical byte counts, by source-level count of the state load/stores),
  launch-order locality (rewriting the grid to the other kernel's order gained
  0.75%), and store cache policy (`.cs` to `.wt`, slightly worse). What remains is
  the register layout and reduction structure — a different algorithm, not a
  tuning constant. 

### End to end (companion SGLang PR)

Un-profiled, random dataset ISL/OSL 1024/1024, `num-prompts == max-concurrency`.

| conc | baseline tok/s | with this op | delta | baseline TPOT | with op TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 459.9 | 487.4 | **+6.0%** | 4.27 ms | 4.03 ms |
| 8 | 3072.1 | 3262.3 | **+6.2%** | 5.07 ms | 4.76 ms |
| 32 | 8858.2 | 9666.3 | **+9.1%** | 6.86 ms | 6.26 ms |
| 64 | 13974.7 | 15109.6 | **+8.1%** | 8.60 ms | 7.91 ms |

GSM8K 1319q: 0.941 baseline vs 0.941 with the op, `Invalid: 0.000` on both.

  ### End to end at a raised graph cap

  The large-batch band only fires above batch 128, which requires
  `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode` above its default of 64. At a cap of 256, two arms
  on the same base, un-profiled:                         

  | conc | baseline tok/s | with this op | delta | baseline TPOT | with op TPOT |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|                              
  | 128 | 21528.0 | 22596.2 | **+5.0%** | 11.00 ms | 10.43 ms |
  | 256 | 30926.3 | 32276.3 | **+4.4%** | 14.97 ms | 14.29 ms |

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run --rm -it --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri --network host \
  --group-add video --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  -v $HF_HOME:/hf lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910

pytest op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py -q
```

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added, mirroring the op tree (`op_tests/triton_tests/`)
- [x] `black` / `ruff` clean
- [x] DCO sign-off on every commit
- [x] gfx950-gated; no CUDA path affected
- [x] Benchmark (`op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`)

body:
## Motivation

Follow-up to [PR #3913](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/3913) (dense FP8 MQA-logits FlyDSL). This PR adds the **paged / decode** lightning-indexer path for **gfx950 (CDNA4)**.

The DeepSeek indexer produces sparse-attention selection logits during decode. For each query row `m` and KV position `n`:

    logits[m, n] = sum_h ReLU(<Q[m, h, :], K[n, :]> * kv_scale[n]) * weights[m, h]

`Q` and `K` are fp8 e4m3; `weights`, `kv_scale`, and the output are f32. K and its per-token scale are co-packed in a **preshuffled paged cache** (`KVBlockSize=64`) and gathered through a block table.

### Ragged `next_n` for confidence-scheduled verification

The motivation for per-sequence `next_n` is the same problem [vLLM describes for DSpark adaptive verification](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-14-dspark-adaptive-verification) [[1](#references)]: a static `num_speculative_tokens` is not optimal across concurrencies, because “per-position acceptance decays fast” and a low-probability tail token “costs a slot in every verification batch.”

From that post: DSpark’s confidence head “scores each drafted token’s chance of surviving verification,” and the scheduler keeps a **contiguous prefix per request**. “Slots compete across requests: position 5 of a confident request can outrank position 1 of a low-confidence one.” The decode step is therefore **varlen**. vLLM captures graphs with a promised `max_query_len = num_speculative_tokens + 1` so “one graph serves any mix of 1 to `num_speculative_tokens + 1` tokens per request.” On SM100 they note that this needs a varlen indexer (DeepGEMM, landed with vLLM PR #47808).

The indexer on gfx950 must follow that mix. Production Gluon `deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` takes one launch-wide `next_n = Q.shape[1]`, so a trimmed batch is either padded to the longest prefix (wasted Q rows and stores) or split into homogeneous launches. This kernel accepts:

- compact `Q[B, next_n, 32, 128]` with `next_n ∈ {1..8}` (same packed layout as Gluon; no forced pad to 8)
- optional `next_n_lens[B]`, each in `{1..next_n}`: live rows for sequence `b` are the leading `min(next_n_lens[b], next_n)` rows
- unused logit rows stay `-inf`

The compiled kernel still reserves LDS for eight rows (one binary, graph-capture friendly). The compute loop early-exits when `row >= nn`, so a confidence-trimmed sequence does not replay MFMA / stores for discarded draft slots. That is the gfx950 counterpart of the varlen indexer vLLM cites for SM100 [[1](#references)].

**Scope:** gfx942 / KVBlockSize=1 / H=64 were explored earlier in the branch and dropped. The landed kernel is gfx950 H=32 D=128 KVB=64 only.

## Technical details

**Kernel:** `aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/mqa_logits/fp8_paged_mqa_logits_gfx950.py`
**Public entry:** `flydsl_fp8_paged_mqa_logits` (re-exported from `mqa_logits/fp8_paged_mqa_logits.py`)

- **Dynamic `next_n`:** `rows_per_batch` from `Q.shape[1]`; `nn = rows_per_batch` if `next_n_lens` is omitted, else `min(next_n_lens[b], rows_per_batch)`. Q/W LDS fill and logit stores are indexed with `pid_batch * rows_per_batch + row`.
- **8-wave CTA (512 threads):** waves 0–3 each own one N=16 tile of a 64-token page and loop **live** Q rows; waves 4–7 NT-G2L the next page into the idle LDS bank (`aux=2`).
- **MFMA:** `v_mfma_scale_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4` via `fx.make_mma_atom` + `fx.gemm`. H=32 is two M-atoms. ReLU·w, `shuffle_xor(16/32)`, lanes 0–15 NT-store.
- **LDS:** 50,688 B (2×8,448 K banks + 32 KiB Q + 1 KiB W) → occupancy **3 WG/CU**.
- **SplitKV:** `min(real_pages, ceil(total_cu * 3 / B))` targeting that occupancy. Explicit `SplitKV` remains graph-capture safe.
- **Pages in HBM** are always 64 tokens.

Visualization of the algorithm:
![vis](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/299473839/652252736-18d71276-bdfe-4a46-b602-6ba29999b1d5.jpg?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJnaXRodWIuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoicmF3LmdpdGh1YnVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbSIsImtleSI6ImtleTUiLCJleHAiOjE3OTAwNzY0OTEsIm5iZiI6MTc5MDA3NjE5MSwicGF0aCI6Ii8yOTk0NzM4MzkvNjUyMjUyNzM2LTE4ZDcxMjc2LWJkZmUtNGE0Ni1iNjAyLTZiYTI5OTk5YjFkNS5qcGc_.shmuApDTztnjC-aIkRh-C28I-QFx4JawcDV_xEOOsrw)

## Test plan

- `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_fp8_paged_mqa_logits.py` — gfx950 correctness vs torch port of vLLM `fp8_paged_mqa_logits_torch`. Gate: exact `-inf` mask + `calc_diff < 1e-3`.
- `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_gfx950.py` — long-context / SplitKV / wide-output cases, including ragged `next_n_lens`.
- `op_tests/flydsl_tests/test_flydsl_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_ragged_nn.py` — compact uniform `next_n ∈ {1,2,4,8}` **and** mixed `next_n_lens` in one batch (unused rows stay `-inf`; mutating padded Q rows must not change live logits).

## Performance (MI355X / gfx950)

Workload is the Probe_1079 decode histogram: 212 calls, 137 unique Nq (1..256, mean 117.1), scattered `randperm` pages, KV pool 44362 blocks, `max_model_len=258048`. 10 iters / 3 warmup. Times in µs.

**Ragged mix (FlyDSL-only).** Per-sequence `next_n_lens` sampled in 1..8 (mean 4.56, mean live Q rows 528). This is the confidence-trim shape: one launch, heterogeneous prefixes. Gluon has no `next_n_lens` and would have to pad to 8 or split launches.

    ctx=8192     FlyDSL  71.40 µs
    ctx=131072   FlyDSL  1067.41 µs

**Uniform compact vs Gluon** (`deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits`, Triton 3.7.0, `ChunkK=256`, `WavePerEU=2`). Same Nq mix; both backends get `Q[:, next_n]`. Ratio is **Gluon / FlyDSL** (>1 means FlyDSL is faster).

```
              ctx=8192 (128 pages)              ctx=131072 (2048 pages)
 next_n     FlyDSL     Gluon    G/F          FlyDSL      Gluon     G/F
     1       37.04     23.22   0.627          585.64     296.28   0.506
     2       39.38     39.57   1.005          608.45     565.08   0.929
     3       48.54     55.66   1.147          680.81     838.12   1.231
     4       57.44     72.34   1.259          836.65    1114.54   1.332
     5       66.69     88.77   1.331          975.66    1386.87   1.421
     6       76.27    105.25   1.380         1129.98    1672.09   1.480
     7       87.19    122.00   1.399         1303.14    1947.69   1.495
     8       97.44    138.12   1.418         1471.31    2224.44   1.512
```

Crossover is **nn≈2 at 8k** and **between nn=2 and nn=3 at 128k**. Gluon wins at a uniform `next_n=1`; FlyDSL pulls ahead as more Q rows reuse each fetched page. Under the adaptive-verification mix described in [[1](#references)], mean `next_n` is not the pad width: our ragged numbers (mean nn=4.56) sit between the uniform nn=4 and nn=5 columns rather than at padded nn=8.

## References

1. vLLM Team, “[Adaptive Verification in vLLM: DSpark confidence-scheduled verification](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-14-dspark-adaptive-verification),” 14 Aug 2026.

title: [Triton/Gluon] gfx942: dtype-split large-prefill attn_2d entries for head 256/512 (Gemma-4)
body:
## Summary

Adds four `attn_2d` entries to the gfx942 unified-attention table so large prefill on head-256/512 layers (Gemma-4-31B: 10 full-attention layers at head 512, sliding layers at head 256) stops running on the decode-era `BLOCK_M=16` configs. Continues and supersedes the config side of #5063, informed by a side-by-side with #5649.

```json
"D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_1024.DT_fp8_fp8":  {"BLOCK_M": 128, "num_warps": 8, "num_stages": 2, "waves_per_eu": 2, "TILE_SIZE_MIN": 16, "TILE_SIZE_MAX": 16},
"D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_1024.DT_bf16_bf16": {"BLOCK_M": 64, "num_warps": 8, "num_stages": 2, "waves_per_eu": 2, "TILE_SIZE_MIN": 16, "TILE_SIZE_MAX": 16},
"D_GEQ_256.Q_GEQ_1024.DT_fp8_fp8":  {"BLOCK_M": 64, "num_warps": 2, "num_stages": 2, "waves_per_eu": 2, "TILE_SIZE_MIN": 16, "TILE_SIZE_MAX": 16},
"D_GEQ_256.Q_GEQ_1024.DT_bf16_bf16": {"BLOCK_M": 64, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 2, "waves_per_eu": 2, "TILE_SIZE_MIN": 16, "TILE_SIZE_MAX": 16}
```

## Why dtype-split

The two prior attempts at this used dtype-agnostic composite keys. Measured on MI325X (isolated kernel bench, same kernel body for every arm — only `select_2d_config`'s return is swapped; Gemma-4 per-rank shapes 32q/4kv, page 64, 16k tokens, median `do_bench`):

**fp8 q+kv (D=512, 16k tokens):**

| arm | ms | regs / spills |
|---|---|---|
| table `D_GEQ_512.DT_fp8_fp8` (M16/T32/w4) | 43.6 | 211 / 0 |
| #5649 `D_GEQ_512.Q_GEQ_256` (M64/T16/w4) | 25.7 | 256 / 0 |
| **new fp8 entry (M128/T16/w8)** | **18.9** | 238 / 0 |

**bf16 (D=512, 16k tokens):**

| arm | ms |
|---|---|
| table `D_GEQ_512` (M16/T16/w4) | 69.9 |
| #5649 entry applied to bf16 (M64/T16/w4) | **93.0 — regression** (CI triton 3.8.0) |
| **new bf16 entry (M64/T16/w8)** | **38.8** |

The fp8-tuned warp count regresses bf16, and BLOCK_M 128 at bf16 overflows the 64KB LDS (compile error, required 131072). So the entries are split on `DT`.

**D=256 sliding-window prefill (SW=1024, 16k tokens):**

| dtype | table (M16/T32/w4) | new entry |
|---|---|---|
| fp8 | 3.32 | **1.21** (M64/T16/w2) |
| bf16 | 4.49 | **1.84** (M64/T16/w4) |

## Why Q_GEQ_1024

Measured crossover vs the D-only entries is between 512 and 1024 tokens (at Q=512 the D-only entries still win on both dtypes; at Q=1024 the composites win). Binding at 256 (as #5649 does) gives the new configs sub-1k-token prefills where they slightly lose; binding at 1024 leaves those on the existing entries.

## Pre-shuffled KV note

The pre-shuffled A8W8 path pins `TILE_SIZE = block_size` after lookup (`unified_attention.py`, `_unified_attention_2d_triton`). With block_size 64 at head 512, M64/T64 needs 69632B of LDS — over the 65536B limit — so this entry must not be used as-is there; measured M16/T64 (the current effective config for that path) compiles and runs. The new keys are dtype-scoped to plain fp8/bf16 KV; the pre-shuffled path should get its own entry after a dedicated tuning pass (not attempted here).

## Verification

- Isolated kernel bench on MI325X, both triton 3.7.1 (vllm-openai-rocm v0.28.0 image) and **3.8.0 (aiter CI pin, installed from pypi.amd.com)**: numbers above are from 3.8.0; 3.7.1 agrees within ~5%.
- Register/spill stats via kernel `n_regs`/`n_spills`: every new entry compiles with 0 spills (M128/w8 fp8: 238 regs, LDS exactly 65536B).
- Lookup regression tests: `op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_unified_attention_config.py` asserts the matched key and BLOCK_M for all 18 cases (both dtypes × both head tiers × decode controls × Q=1023/1024 boundary), run against the actual `_lookup`/`_axis_values` from this branch — 18/18 pass.
- Output equivalence between arms verified in-bench (max abs diff at fp8 = 1 quant step of the synthetic input scale; 0 at bf16).

## Pre-shuffled KV (follow-up commit)

The SHUF axis was added to the schema so pre-shuffled A8W8 prefill (where the wrapper pins `TILE_SIZE = block_size` post-lookup) gets LDS-safe, separately tuned entries: head 512 `M32/w4/s1` (42.2 → 28.6 ms) and head 256 `M128/w8/s2` (16.6 → 9.1 ms), both fp8, MI325X. Six shuffled lookup cases cover Copilot's ask; 24/24 total pass.

title: [HIP] [CI] [JIT] [Feature] Add gfx:cu_num build targets so one build serves multiple SKUs of an arch
body:
## Motivation

AITER selects tuned GEMM kernels at build time using `(gfx, cu_num, ...)`. GPUs sharing an architecture can have different CU counts. For example, `gfx950` with 128 CUs on MI350P and 256 CUs on MI350X/MI355X. `GPU_ARCHS` and a single global `CU_NUM` cannot request both configurations in one build. This PR adds `AITER_GPU_TARGETS="gfx950:128;gfx950:256"` so the existing code-generation path can include tuned kernels for both targets. It provides the target-selection mechanism; corresponding tuning data is still required.

`AITER_GPU_TARGETS` is optional. Builds that leave it unset continue to use `GPU_ARCHS`, `CU_NUM`, or native detection, but this PR also changes some of their behavior:

- For explicitly named `GPU_ARCHS` targets, omitting `CU_NUM` previously selected each architecture's default CU count; it now uses the live device's count for the matching architecture, retaining defaults for other targets or when detection fails.
- For multiple named architectures, `get_gfx()` previously selected the last entry; it now selects the detected architecture if included, otherwise the lexicographically greatest name, making the fallback independent of list order.
- Explicit `GPU_ARCHS` builds previously accepted zero and negative `CU_NUM` overrides; now only positive integers are accepted.
- `_parse_gpu_archs_env` previously preserved architecture-name case; it now normalizes names to lowercase, so entries such as `GFX942` resolve as `gfx942`.

## Build target resolution

| `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` | `GPU_ARCHS` | `CU_NUM` | Build targets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gfx950:128;gfx950:256` | ignored | ignored | `gfx950:128`, `gfx950:256` |
| `gfx942;gfx950:128` | ignored | ignored | `gfx942:304`, `gfx950:128` |
| unset | `gfx942;gfx950` | unset | `gfx942:304`, `gfx950:256`[^cu] |
| unset | `gfx942;gfx950` | `80` | `gfx942:80`, `gfx950:80` |
| unset | `gfx950` | unset, no GPU | `gfx950:256` |
| unset | unset or `native` | unset | live architecture at its live CU count |
| unset | unset or `native` | `80` | live architecture at `80` |
| unset | unset or `native` | any, no GPU | error |

[^cu]: The architecture matching the live device takes that device's CU count.

`CU_NUM` applies to every architecture named in `GPU_ARCHS`. A bare `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` entry takes its
architecture's default count. When `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` is set, a `GPU_ARCHS` naming a different architecture set warns. A `CU_NUM` matching none of the targets warns.

## Implementation/Changes

- **Target parsing and selection.** `build_targets.py` parses `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` into `(gfx, cu_num)` pairs, validates architecture names and positive CU counts, and removes exact duplicates. Entries without a CU count use the architecture default. These pairs replace `GPU_ARCHS`/`CU_NUM` for build-target selection and feed the existing CSV filtering, so two CU counts of one architecture can both contribute tuned rows.

- **Architecture validation and gfx1250 flags.** `jit/core.py` and `cpp_itfs/utils.py` derive compiler architecture lists from the new targets when set. Both validators use `KNOWN_GFX` instead of separate allowlists. The gfx1250 compiler flags and cluster-launch define check membership in `get_gfx_list()` instead of reading `GPU_ARCHS` directly; cluster launch still requires ROCm 7.0 or later.

- **Template-library cache keys.** C++ template-library cache paths now include the sorted, deduplicated architecture set. Different sets use separate caches; `gfx950;gfx942`, `gfx942;gfx950`, and equivalent lists with duplicates share one. Paged-attention AOT temporary files and locks use the same key. Existing template libraries rebuild under the new paths on first use. The main JIT module cache is unchanged and does not distinguish CU counts.

- **HSACO and MLA assembly paths.** HSACO cache reads and default writes use `get_gfx_runtime()`, as does MLA assembly lookup. This replaces paths based on the raw `GPU_ARCHS` value, which could contain multiple architecture names.

- **Warnings and documentation.** Build-target resolution reports when no live CU count can be read, and warns when `CU_NUM` requests a count absent from `AITER_GPU_TARGETS`. CSV filtering warns about targets with no rows for the selected library type; those targets continue to use default kernels. The installation guide documents the new variable and that `CU_NUM` still overrides runtime lookup.

- **Release and nightly workflows.** The reusable release workflow accepts a `gpu_targets` input and passes it into the build containers as `AITER_GPU_TARGETS`. Automated release and default nightly builds specify `gfx942:304;gfx950:256`, so their target CU counts do not depend on the build host.

## Out of scope

OPUS and FlyDSL AOT target-filtering integration and adding the gfx950:128 tuning rows is a separate effort and is out of scope here. This is the `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` mechanism only. Both are addressed in the follow-ups below.

## Test Plan

- Extend GEMM code-generation tests to cover multiple CU counts for one architecture, target deduplication, default counts, environment precedence, and reporting targets without tuned rows.
- Add GPU target-resolution tests with the live GPU probes mocked. Cover live CU detection for a binned part, order-independent architecture selection, gfx1250 compiler flags, and cache separation.
- Run the existing GEMM dispatch/code-generation and JIT-cache transaction regression suites.

## Test Result

Verified on MI300X and MI355X :

- `python op_tests/test_gemm_codegen.py`: 64 checks passed, 0 failed.
- `python -m pytest -q op_tests/test_gpu_target_resolution.py op_tests/test_jit_cache_transaction.py`: 56 tests passed, 0 failed.


## Follow-up PRs

 * #5668, to key the opus MXFP8 BMM lookup on CU count.
 * #5342 to filter FlyDSL GEMM AOT jobs by build target.

title: [FlyDSL] [Feature] Precompile only the GEMM kernels the wheel is built for
body:
Stops a released wheel from precompiling FlyDSL GEMM kernels for architectures it is not built for. The packaging path compiled every job in the tuned CSVs regardless of the wheel's targets; it now filters by build target, the way the standalone entry point already did.

Stacked on #5340, which introduces `AITER_GPU_TARGETS`: build targets written as `gfx:cu_num` pairs. The filter here resolves through that machinery, so packaging selects AOT jobs the way the rest of the build selects tuned rows.

## Motivation

`setup.py` → `run_aot()` → `_collect_aot_jobs_for()` called `collect_aot_jobs()` with no target filter, so approximately 220 gfx1250 kernels were built into every gfx942/gfx950 wheel, which never reaches them. The same gap shows up on MI350P: FlyDSL dispatch keys on `(gfx, cu_num)` from the live device, and every tuned FlyDSL row records 256 CUs, so on a 128-CU part every lookup misses, yet a `gfx950:128` build was precompiling all of those kernels anyway. It now selects none of them, and once rows are tuned for 128 CUs it will select exactly those. 


### Scope

GEMM only. Each other `OpKind` reads its own CSVs and keeps only one of the two fields a target needs: MoE and chunk_gdn_h carry `cu_num` and recover an arch later through `cu_num_to_arch`, grouped MoE carries `gfx` alone, mxfp4 MoE hardcodes `FLYDSL_GPU_ARCH` to gfx950, and mega MoE builds its jobs without a CSV. Matching those jobs against a `(gfx, cu_num)` pair would drop every one. Filtering them means widening each `parse_csv` to carry both fields, plus a `gfx` column for the mxfp4 model CSVs that lack one, which is out of scope here.


## Technical Details


**1. Packaging now resolves targets the way CK does; the standalone entry point still does not.** CK's codegen resolves `GPU_ARCHS` and `CU_NUM` into exact `(gfx, cu_num)` pairs and keeps only the tuned rows matching them. FlyDSL packaging did none of that, baking every row in the CSVs whatever the build targeted. It now resolves the same pairs, so both halves of a build select for the same SKU.

The standalone entry point is unchanged: it still matches on architecture alone and ignores `CU_NUM`. Only that divergence is now visible. Under `GPU_ARCHS=gfx950 CU_NUM=128` packaging selects nothing, since every FlyDSL GEMM row records 256 CUs, while the CLI selects every gfx950 job. Neither result is wrong on its own, and an AOT miss only falls back to a runtime JIT compile, but one environment now means two different things depending on which entry point reads it. 

**2. An unknown arch now fails the build.** `GPU_ARCHS=gfx9999` raises, aborting the wheel build where packaging previously ignored the variable and baked everything. Intended, but it is a hard failure on a free-form `workflow_dispatch` input. Every in-tree caller passes a valid value and `gpu_archs` has a default, so no automated path can hit it.

**3. The filter reads `AITER_GPU_TARGETS` and `GPU_ARCHS` only.** `ARCH` stays on the standalone entry point: build images export it as a machine type such as `x86_64`, and an unrecognised value raises, so routing packaging through it would kill the wheel build on those hosts.

**4. Uppercase now matches where it previously matched nothing.** Case-folding means `GFX950` selects every gfx950 job where it used to select none. On the packaging path that is a narrowing, since it baked every job in the CSVs before reading no target variable at all; on the standalone entry point it is the opposite, since an unmatched arch there selected nothing and fell back to runtime JIT.


### Also in here

A release build gains one warning line naming gfx942, correct since no `libtype=flydsl` GEMM rows exist for it. `parse_csv` no longer raises on an empty `cu_num` cell; it parses as 0, which the filter treats as a wildcard. No shipped CSV trips this today.

## Test Plan

`op_tests/test_gemm_codegen.py`, covering the packaging collector end to end, partial target coverage, legacy rows with no `gfx`, both separator forms, and each rejected `GPU_ARCHS` input.

## Test Result

Passes; `ruff` and `black` clean. An AOT miss is not a failure, it falls back to a runtime JIT compile, so `AITER_GPU_TARGETS=gfx950:128` selecting 0 jobs today is safe.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Perf] Shallow-copy GEMM configs instead of deep-copying them
body:
`get_gemm_config()` returns `copy.deepcopy(config)` of a bucket dict it took
from an `lru_cache`. The copy is load-bearing — callers mutate what they get
back, `compute_splitk_params()` in place and the gluon paths via
`config.pop("kernel_type")` — but every value in a GEMM bucket is a scalar, so
`dict(entry)` isolates the cached entry identically. `copy.deepcopy` takes its
atomic fast path for `int`/`str`/`bool`/`None`, so both copies hand the kernel
the *same* value objects: nothing downstream can observe the difference.

This is the rule the repo already states in `configs/CLAUDE.md` and
`.github/instructions/aiter-ops-triton.instructions.md` — "`dict(...)` for flat
entries, `copy.deepcopy` for nested ones" — and the one `get_conv_config()`
already follows, its docstring saying it is modeled on `get_gemm_config()` and
that "a deep copy only adds hot-path overhead". `get_gemm_config()` is the
shared loader for ~28 Triton GEMM kernels and runs once per launch.

## Micro

gfx950 MI355X, torch 2.12.0+git6bbd260, `d483dbf` against `d483dbf` + this
change, single tenant on an otherwise idle host. Host wall-clock on the dispatch
path, calls issued back to back without syncing; `do_bench` reports kernel time
and is blind to this. Four interleaved pairs with the order alternated, pair 0
discarded, median of the other three; 6 shapes × 4000 iterations × 9 repeats.
The trailing-`synchronize()` drain stayed at 0.005–0.014 µs/call across all 72
kept points, so the host is what was timed.

| | base | patched | | per-shape range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `get_gemm_config()` alone | 2.46 µs | 0.12 µs | **−95.1 %** | 92.3–95.2 % |
| `gemm_a16w16()` dispatch | 27.35 µs | 24.90 µs | **−8.7 %** | 8.3–9.9 % |
| `gemm_afp4wfp4()` dispatch | 37.42 µs | 33.87 µs | **−9.1 %** | 8.0–9.7 % |

The two GEMM families agree because each pays exactly one copy per launch: about
2.4 µs, which is 9 % of their host dispatch. The outlier shape in the first row
is M=23, which lands in a bucket whose lookup is itself slower.

## Engine startup

The one place the change has a measurable effect under vLLM's defaults. Timing
the function itself across a full `LLM()` init of gpt-oss-120b, rather than
looking for it in wall-clock startup, which weight I/O dominates:

| | calls | time in `get_gemm_config` |
|---|---|---|
| base | 51 156 | 408.8 / 397.8 ms |
| patched | 51 156 | 55.5 / 56.8 ms |

Two repeats each; the call count is identical by construction. About 345 ms per
engine start, 0.4–0.5 % of init.

## What reaches this code

Counted by instrumenting `get_gemm_config` inside the aiter tree, so
tensor-parallel workers are included, rather than inferred from config files:

| model | calls | family |
|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-120b | 51 156 at startup, 0 per decode step | `GEMM-A16W16` |
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct | 4 200 at startup, 0 per decode step | `BATCHED_GEMM-A16WFP4` |
| Qwen3-14B-FP8, MiniMax-M2.7 | 0 | — |

Under vLLM's default HIP-graph path a decode step makes no calls at all;
`--enforce-eager` on gpt-oss gives 108 per step. So the win lands on startup,
prefill, graph capture, eager execution, tuning sweeps and callers outside vLLM,
and **cannot** move graph-mode decode throughput.

## End to end

`vllm bench serve`, TP=1, ISL 2000 / OSL 150, 60 prompts, concurrency 24,
interleaved pairs with the order alternated and pair 0 discarded. Included to
show nothing regresses; by the counts above it cannot show a gain.

**Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct**, 5 kept pairs, with an **A/A control** — the
base build against a second copy of itself, given the same separate cache roots
the real pair gets:

| | per-pair Δ tok/s | band |
|---|---|---|
| base vs patched | −3.46 −4.10 +0.76 −3.72 +0.44 | −4.1 … +0.8 % |
| base vs base (A/A) | −0.99 +0.91 +3.08 +5.02 | −1.0 … +5.0 % |

Throughput on this model is bimodal: 5 of 18 runs land near 21 500 tok/s instead
of 22 400. Three are the patched arm — and **two are an unpatched arm in the A/A
control**, which is what rules the patch out. The bands are the same width, so
this harness cannot resolve anything below about 5 % here.

TTFT does resolve, and it is the metric prefill lives in:

| | base | patched | Δ | spreads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean TTFT (ms) | 475.2 | 475.7 | +0.10 % | 0.9 % / 0.5 % |
| Median TTFT (ms) | 483.0 | 482.4 | −0.12 % | 0.6 % / 0.6 % |

**gpt-oss-120b**, 5 converged pairs (its first two are warmup — one base run came
in at 6 838 tok/s): total 28 800 → 28 866 tok/s (+0.23 %, base spread 5.1 %),
mean TPOT 7.46 → 7.43 ms, mean TTFT 461.7 → 456.9 ms.

## Accuracy

`lm_eval` GSM8K, 5-shot greedy, all 1319 items, `max_model_len=4096`,
`max_gen_toks=256`, `enable_prefix_caching=False`, `seed=1234`. `base2` is a
second run of the **unpatched** build, so its delta is the harness's noise floor.

| model | strict base | patched | Δ patch | Δ base-repeat | stderr | identical text base→patched | base→base |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-120b | 0.2699 | 0.2714 | +0.0015 | +0.0197 | ±0.0122 | 2.0 % | 1.5 % |
| Qwen3-Next-80B (0 calls) | 0.8105 | 0.8249 | +0.0144 | +0.0083 | ±0.0108 | 37.1 % | 33.7 % |

On the affected model a repeat of the unpatched build moves the score 13× further
than the patch does, and in both models the patched arm reproduces base's text at
least as often as base reproduces its own. Same-verdict rate is 71.9 % and 94.6 %.
gpt-oss's absolute score is low because `strict-match` does not fit its output
format; only the within-model comparison is read here.

No measurable accuracy change on GSM8K, within the base-repeat noise floor. GSM8K
exercises one shape of one path and says nothing about long context, sampling or
multi-turn.

The end-to-end and GSM8K arms also carried two lazy-logging conversions that have
since been split out of this PR. Neither reaches those call sites in any material
number — gpt-oss never calls them, Kimi-Linear calls `dynamic_mxfp4_quant` 14
times in a whole run — so those measurements stand for the change as it ships.

## Tests

`op_tests/triton_tests/gemm/basic/test_gemm_a16w16.py` 360 passed / 648 skipped
and `test_gemm_afp4wfp4.py` 234 passed / 290 skipped, identical on both arms.

`op_tests/triton_tests/test_config_copy_contract.py` is new, and covers more than
this change. Four loaders return `dict(entry)` of an `lru_cache`d object —
`get_gemm_config`, `get_conv_config`, `get_mhc_config`, `get_mhc_post_config` —
and nothing tested that contract for any of them. A nested value in any of their
tables would be shared between the cache and the caller, and a caller mutating it
in place would poison every later lookup of that shape, with no exception raised.

Three layers: the shipped gemm, conv and mhc tables are walked for **every**
architecture rather than the one running the test; the loaders are driven to
check the isolation itself, since reading the tables alone would still pass if a
loader returned the cached object; and an inventory test fails when a new
`dict(entry)` loader appears without coverage, so this tracks the source instead
of freezing at the set that exists today.

It was run against six deliberately wrong trees, each of which takes down a
different subset — a nested value in a gemm bucket, in a conv exact-shape pin and
in an mhc bucket; a typo'd bucket key the walk does not recognise; a loader that
hands back the cached object (5 of 9); and a new uncovered shallow-copy loader.
All nine pass on the shipped tree.

It lives under `op_tests/triton_tests/` because that is what CI actually
collects — the Triton job pytest-runs that directory recursively on any PR
touching `aiter/ops/triton/**`, which this PR does.

title: add block_cat_fused fused op
body:
Adds a self-contained custom op torch.ops.aiter.block_cat_fused(l12, l4, slope, l1_width) -> Tensor:

    forward : cat([leaky_relu(l12[..., :W1], slope), l12[..., W1:] * l4], dim=-1)
    backward: grad_l12 and grad_l4 in one fused Triton kernel

Registering this as one op, instead of letting the cat / leaky_relu / mul chain decompose, gives AOTAutograd a single fused backward target. Without it the backward decomposes into a pair of pointwise paths that each round-trip the activation through HBM; with it the backward is one kernel and one round-trip. Forward runs a fused Triton kernel on the bf16/fp16 GPU path with an eager torch fallback for CPU/fp32.

Test plan: op_tests/test_block_cat_fused.py covers forward and backward correctness against eager on CPU fp32 (fallback) and GPU bf16 (Triton path).

title: [Triton/Gluon] Drop `GRID_MN` from the batched MXFP4 GEMM specialisation keys
body:
### Motivation

Both batched MXFP4 GEMM kernels take `GRID_MN` as a `tl.constexpr`, fed by a
`@triton.heuristics` lambda over the raw `M` and `N`:

```python
"GRID_MN": lambda args: triton.cdiv(args["M"], args["BLOCK_SIZE_M"])
* triton.cdiv(args["N"], args["BLOCK_SIZE_N"]),
```

That puts `M` into the JIT cache key without passing through
`STANDARD_M_BOUNDS`. Under serving, `M` is the scheduler-formed batch size, so
the key is effectively indexed by batch shape: the kernel mints a new binary
every time a new batch shape appears, and never converges. On
`GLM-5.3-Flash-Quark-MXFP4` (MI355X, TP2, vLLM), `_batched_gemm_a16wfp4_kernel`
built 168 binaries for 10 distinct configs and was still compiling new variants
at repetition 5 of a benchmark.

### Change

Four edits per file:

- Call site: `remap_xcd(pid, GRID_MN)` → `remap_xcd(pid, num_pid_m * num_pid_n)`
- Drop the `GRID_MN` lambda from `@triton.heuristics`
- Drop `GRID_MN: tl.constexpr` from the kernel signature
- Drop `"GRID_MN"` from the `make_kernel_repr` list

`num_pid_m` and `num_pid_n` are already computed in-body from the same `M`,
`N`, `BLOCK_SIZE_M`, `BLOCK_SIZE_N`, so the value is identical; `remap_xcd` is
pure index arithmetic and both call sites discard its return. Same binaries,
far fewer of them. No tuning configs are touched.

### Precedent

- **#2427** made exactly this change — same four edits — to `gemm_a16w16` and
  to `batched_gemm_a8w8_a_per_token_group_prequant_w_per_batched_tensor_quant`,
  under the title "for no recompile".
- **#4199** did it for `gemm_a8w8_blockscale`, but bundled a re-tune of 12
  config JSONs. This PR changes no configs.
- `gemm/basic/gemm_afp4wfp4.py:88` already computes the same value in-body
  rather than as a constexpr, so the in-body form is already in the tree.

### Evidence

Six vLLM servers, three GPU pairs, started together on an idle host. Each
server runs one config (512×512 tokens, concurrency 16) for 6 repetitions.
Throughput is output tokens/s; "steady" is the mean of reps 3–6.

| build | GPUs | rep 1 tok/s | steady tok/s | rep‑1 vs steady | rep‑1 wall | compiles per rep | after rep 1 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `main` | 0,2 | 217.1 | 372.7 | **−41.8%** | 25.56 s | 60, 8, 8, 8, 4, 0 | 28 |
| `main` | 1,3 | 227.4 | 386.8 | **−41.2%** | 24.40 s | 54, 4, 4, 4, 0, 0 | 12 |
| `main` | 4,6 | 239.9 | 375.6 | **−36.1%** | 23.13 s | 50, 0, 0, 8, 8, 0 | 16 |
| this PR | 0,2 | **405.1** | 400.2 | **+1.2%** | **13.70 s** | **14, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | **0** |
| this PR | 1,3 | **402.2** | 407.6 | **−1.3%** | **13.79 s** | **14, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | **0** |
| this PR | 4,6 | **385.2** | 399.9 | **−3.7%** | **14.40 s** | **14, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0** | **0** |

Totals: **220 → 42** compilations during the run, **56 → 0** after repetition 1.
Compiles per rep are counted by snapshotting the compile-cache directories at
each repetition boundary and diffing the new entries.

- The first-repetition cost is removed, not reduced — on all three pairs. The
  residual 14 are unrelated kernels compiled once at startup; this PR's arms
  build no `_batched_gemm_a16wfp4_kernel` variants at all.
- `main` never converges: it is still compiling at repetition 5. This PR
  compiles once, then never again.
- The cost is not confined to repetition 1: `main`'s steady figures (372–387)
  are themselves depressed by continued compilation. Averaging only the
  repetitions that provably compiled nothing puts `main` at 398–404 against
  this PR's 399–409 — steady-state performance is unchanged.

Across a wider six-config sweep on a single server, total compilations fell
285 → 35 (−88%).

### Testing

`op_tests/triton_tests/gemm/batched/test_batched_gemm_a16wfp4.py` and
`test_batched_gemm_afp4wfp4.py`, same container and GPUs, kernels swapped
between runs: **4977 passed, 0 failed** on both `origin/main` and this branch.

### Not included

- **`do_not_specialize=["M", "N"]`**, which #2427 also added. It removes zero
  compilations here (29 vs 33) — what remains after `GRID_MN` is Triton's
  bounded divisibility specialisation, paid once at startup — and costs
  0.9–2.5% throughput, the regression #2482 had to repair with `EVEN_MN`.
- **The other 15 files declaring `GRID_MN: tl.constexpr`.** Seven discard
  `remap_xcd`'s return identically and three never read the parameter at all;
  the rest need more care. This PR covers only the two batched MXFP4 files.

### Notes

The measured workload exercises `batched_gemm_a16wfp4` only —
`batched_gemm_afp4wfp4` never compiled during these runs. It is changed here
because it carries the identical heuristic, signature and discarded-return call
site, so the same cost applies wherever it is exercised; it is covered by the
tests above.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used; the author has reviewed and validated the
change.

title: [MHA] Add tuned-config dispatch and delta-race tuner for packed varlen
body:
## Motivation

PR #5592 adds a gfx942 split-KV ASM kernel and picks its split count from a rule of thumb compiled into C++.
But it cannot discover that CK, Triton, Gluon, FlyDSL or OPUS would be faster for a given attention shape. 
This PR lets dispatch look up a choice that was actually measured on that GPU, and adds the tuner that produces those measurements.

## What this PR adds

- A tuned-config lookup in `flash_attn_varlen_func` for packed-varlen MHA forward.
- A tuner, `op_tests/tuners/tune_mha_fwd.py`, with `exhaustive`, `race` and `smoke` strategies.
- Two shipped rows: gfx942 / mi325x, hd192, `asm_v3` split 3, for `return_lse` 0 and 1, measured by @amd-yashagar.

## Technical Details

**Lookup**

- Exact key of `(gfx, gpu_model, cu_num)` plus the problem's 30 shape and dtype fields into `aiter/configs/tuned_mha_fwd.csv`, pinning `(backend, num_splits, backend_config)`.
- Anything else falls through to today's C++ auto-select, so untuned shapes behave as on `main`, at about 2.5 us per call.
- A row is a hint, not a correctness contract: if no kernel gate can honor it, dispatch warns and falls back.

**Backends.** All six are arch-gated in `aiter/ops/mha_fwd_policy.py`, and each was driven through the tuner one at a time on gfx950 / MI355X against the shipped shape, with the correctness and arch gates live:

| backend | on gfx950 |
| --- | --- |
| opus, ck, triton, gluon | ran, passed the correctness gate |
| asm_v3 | ran and passed at split 1; splits 2-8 refused by the split-KV policy, which is gfx942 hd192 only |
| flydsl | gfx1250 only, and no gfx1250 hardware was available here |

Five of six run, flydsl is the one we have no hardware to reach, and a rejected or failing candidate never reaches the published table. `ck` is CK at its own default tiling, for the reason under Related PRs. One number is the reason to tune at all: across the gluon tile configs sampled here, latency spans a factor of 28.

**Tuner**

- `MhaFwdTuner` subclasses `TunerCommon`, the same base as the CK and OPUS GEMM tuners, so the untuned-CSV-in / tuned-CSV-out contract and the CLI are the familiar ones.
- Every candidate is correctness-gated before timing, then measured through `mp_tuner`, one fresh process each.
- `exhaustive` (default) times the whole catalogue to full depth. `race` draws from that same catalogue but measures in randomized short blocks, dropping a candidate once it is proven more than delta worse than the leader: 104 s against 315 s on the 200-candidate field, a **3x wall-clock saving**. `smoke` samples each tile grid and says so in its evidence.
- The race core in `aiter/utility/block_race.py` is family-agnostic.

**Incumbency**

- We want to avoid changing the tuning table if not strictly necessary, hence we always want to compare to the currently selected kernel, i.e. the "incumbent".
- A challenger must beat it by a margin: delta (2% by default) under `race`, twice the combined standard error (about 95%) under `exhaustive`, otherwise no (new) row is published.

**Evidence and resuming**

- A race records every finished measurement block in a journal, so `--resume` picks an interrupted run up where it stopped. Resuming is only sound for the same race, so the journal's filename hashes the shape, the candidate list, the race thresholds, etc to distinguish one tuning run from the other.
- A candidate that faults or returns a latency that is not positive and finite leaves the field with a `crash` verdict; it neither takes the run down nor wins on a broken number.
- Measurements stay out of the dispatch table (measurements are noisy and needlessly grow file size of the lookup table). They go to their own CSV, journal and manifest, and the runtime reader rejects any file carrying measurement columns.

**Shared infrastructure**

Three files outside the MHA path changed because this tuner needed them, and they are worth a separate look from their owners:

- `aiter/utility/mp_tuner.py` (@yzhou103): the worker pool now restarts after a fault and collects per-candidate progress for every caller, so a candidate that crashes the worker costs only itself instead of every measurement already finished for that shape.
- `aiter/utility/base_tuner.py` (@yzhou103): shared tuner CLI and CSV plumbing.
- `aiter/jit/file_baton.py` (@Lingpeng-Jin): detects a lock left behind by a zombie process, which a multi-hour tune hits and a short build does not.


## Test Plan

- `python3 -m unittest` over the eight GPU-free modules registered in `.github/workflows/tuning-tests.yaml` at levels 0 and 1: key derivation and lookup, policy and arch gating, race elimination, incumbency and promotion, journal binding and replay.
- `op_tests/tuning_tests/test_mha_store_agreement.py` on gfx950: ASM and Triton resolve the same table to the same launch, and a tuned row genuinely displaces the C++ auto-select rather than coinciding with it.
- `op_tests/test_fmha_gfx942_asm_splitkv.py` on gfx942, including the CSV-override case and the no-CSV fallback.

## Test Result

- 186 tests in 7.3 s, all passing; store agreement passes on a locked MI355X; `ruff check .` and `black` are clean.

## Related PRs

- **#5592**: this PR is stacked on it and targets its branch, and will be retargeted to `main` once #5592 merges. It ships the ASM kernel and the compiled-in split rule that this PR replaces with a measured choice for the keyed shapes.
- **#5024**: complementary. Both tune kernel parameters; what differs is where each backend exposes them.
  - This PR tunes, per exact shape, the backend and that backend's per-call parameters: Triton and Gluon `BLOCK_M`, `BLOCK_N`, warps, waves and stages, each config JIT-compiling its own kernel, plus the asm_v3 split count. The result is a dispatch-table row.
  - CK's tile recipe is fixed when the module is built, so no per-call row can set it. #5024 rebuilds CK per candidate tile and emits a JSON that CK reads at codegen time through `CK_TILE_FMHA_FWD_CUSTOM_TUNE_CONFIG_FILE`, the hook from ROCm/rocm-libraries#11298.
  - They compose: with such a JSON deployed, the `ck` this tuner measures is the tuned CK, competing against the tuned Triton, Gluon and ASM configs.

## Credit

The foundation, namely the problem and plan contracts, the first exhaustive tuner, the dispatch plumbing and the Triton tile path, is @amd-yashagar's: of the 6188 lines added on this branch, 3821 are his.

title: [FlyDSL] gfx1201 (RDNA4) FlyDSL BF16 attention optimizations & FP8 attention implementation
body:
## Motivation

I am in the process of improving gfx1201 performance in https://github.com/xdit-project/xDiT and turned my focus to attention for some time the past few days.

Diffusion attention (Flux, Wan, SD3.5, etc) is a runtime bottleneck on `gfx1201` (RDNA4). This PR advances the FlyDSL flash-attention path on two fronts:

1. **A faster, more general bf16/f16 kernel.** The existing gfx1201 flash-attention kernel gains shape-driven `(BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N)` tile selection, making it ~**1.09×** faster than the fixed-tile version on `main`. The primary `flydsl_flash_attn_func` also gains **cross-attention** (`seq_q != seq_kv`, previously rejected as self-attention only), **broadened non-causal padding** (tail-masked, beyond main's 0.5% cap, so the production S=32760→32768 case is exact), and `softmax_scale` / `out=` extras.
2. **A new per-tensor fp8 (e4m3) attention path.** fp8 offers real headroom over bf16, but per-tensor scaling is outlier-sensitive, so quality depends on a Hadamard rotation of Q/K to spread channel outliers. This adds the fp8 attention consumer kernel plus a **fully-FlyDSL rotate + quantize producer**, giving up to **2.5–3.0×** over SDPA-flash.

Goals: cut end-to-end attention latency vs SDPA-flash and the prior `main` kernel, with **no accuracy regression**.

## Technical Details

**1. bf16 kernel (`flash_attn_func_gfx1201.py`).**
- **New:** shape-driven `(BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N)` tile selection (`_pick_tiles`): 256/64 for long head_dim=128, 128/32 for short, 128/64 for head_dim<=64 swept on gfx1201.
- **New coverage in `flydsl_flash_attn_func`:** **cross-attention** (`seq_q != seq_kv`; `main` rejected non-equal shapes as self-attention only) and **broadened non-causal padding** — per-column tail masking excludes padded K/V from the softmax, lifting `main`'s 0.5% padding-ratio cap so the production tight-padding case (S=32760→32768) is exact.
- **New API extras** on `flydsl_flash_attn_func`: `softmax_scale`, `out=` buffer reuse, and positional back-compat for the pre-existing signature.

**2. fp8 kernel (new).**
- **Consumer `flash_attn_func_fp8_gfx1201.py`** — per-tensor fp8 (e4m3) flash attention with scalar descales (`real = fp8 * descale`); bf16 output.
- **Producer `fp8_quant_gfx1201.py`** — a 2-pass per-tensor fp8 quant + optional Hadamard rotation, entirely in FlyDSL:
  - pass 1: load + in-register **Fast Walsh–Hadamard Transform** (butterfly wave shuffles, `log2(head_dim)` stages, no matrix load) + per-row amax; a tiny `partials.amax()` gives the global amax with no atomics.
  - pass 2: recompute the FWHT + apply the single global scale + clamp + e4m3 pack.
  - Rotated Q/K never round-trip to HBM (2 reads + 0.5 write). The WHT is orthonormal, so `(Q@R)(K@R)^T == Q@K^T` — it cancels in attention and the consumer never needs the matrix. This default FlyDSL producer runs ~1.24–1.40× faster than the equivalent two-launch Triton (`amax3`+`sc3`) producer, which is also included as the `backend="triton"` fallback.
- **Dispatch (`flydsl_fp8_quant` in `fmha_kernels.py`)** — `backend="flydsl"` (default) uses the new kernels; `"triton"`/`"torch"` remain as fallbacks. The FlyDSL path requires `head_dim==128` (MVP `VEC=4`) and is per-tensor, so q/k/v may differ in size (**cross-attention supported**); other head_dims fall back automatically. The host-side Hadamard matrix is computed lazily (unused on the FlyDSL path). No new environment variables.
- **MVP scope:** `head_dim==128` fast path; `head_dim=64` (sd3.5) falls back to Triton/torch, which handle it correctly. Extending to `VEC=2` only needs the fp8 pack/store generalized; the rest of the kernel is already `VEC`-parametric.

### fp8 rows in the tables below

- **fp8 (incl. quant)** — realistic path: q/k/v arrive bf16, so rotate+quantize is paid **inside** the timed region on every call (the new FlyDSL producer).
- **fp8 (kernel-only)** — attention-kernel ceiling: q/k/v already quantized in HBM (quant amortized upstream), so only attention is timed.

## Test Plan

- **Extensive e2e tests are currently running for various models in 1/2/4 GPU workload configurations along with other improvements I will upstream to xDiT soon and can provide further details here once the full benchmark is complete.**
- **Functional correctness** (`op_tests/test_flydsl_fmha_gfx1201.py`, pytest): bf16/f16/fp8 self- and cross-attention across production shapes, causal, unaligned/tight-padding, out-buffer/softmax-scale, API guards, and **direct producer tests** (scale contract, dequant accuracy, the `(Q@R)(K@R)^T == Q@K^T` rotation-cancellation invariant, and flydsl-vs-torch backend agreement).
- **Performance + VRAM** (`op_tests/test_flydsl_fmha.py`): median latency over `run_perftest` across 5 shapes vs `torch.scaled_dot_product_attention` (FLASH_ATTENTION backend), plus peak/transient VRAM; every timed candidate is cross-checked against an fp32 SDPA reference (`atol=rtol=2e-2`).
- **Environment:** 2× `gfx1201` (RDNA4) Radeon AI PRO R9700 pod. Perf is single-GPU (forward-only, non-causal, `B=1`); the correctness suite runs on both GPUs so the multi-device tests execute. `main bf16` is the bf16 kernel with this PR's tiling/padding changes reverted, measured on the same pod for a like-for-like reference. FLOPs `= 4·B·H·S²·D`; cosine vs fp32 SDPA per `(token,head)` row.

title: [FlyDSL] Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate
body:
# Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate

The decode path now has four candidate kernels and no single one wins the shape space, so this adds the kernel behind a table of measured row intervals keyed by `(arch, CU count, emit, k, width)`. An `(arch, CU count)` pair the table does not name keeps today's behaviour exactly.

## How the dispatch works

Two public entry points reach the decode path, and they do not share a call chain: `topk_select()` routes its `decode` arm straight into the FlyDSL host and never passes through `top_k_per_row_decode()`. So the gate sits in both, and both ask one function rather than deciding for themselves, which is what keeps them from disagreeing about a shape.

```
  top_k_per_row_decode()              topk_select()
  aiter/ops/topk.py                   aiter/ops/topk_select.py
          |                              |- argmax / small_k / plain
          |                              |- stream
          |                              \- decode
          |                                   |
          |                                   v
          |                     flydsl_top_k_per_row_decode()
          |                     aiter/ops/flydsl/topk/topk_per_row.py
          |                                   |
    [gate here]                         [gate here]
          |                                   |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
                            v
              decode_backend_for_call()   <- the only decision
                            |
     +----------------------+---------------------+
     v                      v                     v
  adaptive               chunked              upstream
  (in a band of          (in upstream's       (not ours; the dispatch
   the measured           chunked gate,        below picks the port
   table, looked up       read at the          where enabled, else the
   at the live length)    physical width)      HIP/C++ kernel)
```

The gate never names the fallback kernel itself: it answers "not ours" and upstream's existing dispatch picks, which is the port on gfx950 and gfx1250 and the HIP/C++ kernel elsewhere. That is also why a caller wanting values never reaches the adaptive kernel, which emits indices only. Only `top_k_per_row_decode()` has that dispatch below it. In `topk_select()` the decode arm is already chosen, so "not ours" leaves the chunked kernel.

## `max_row_len`, and what a caller has to pass

A decode buffer is allocated once at the model's maximum context and a call fills whatever part of it the requests need. `seq_lens` is device-resident, so the host cannot read it without a sync, and the adaptive kernel picks its tier, part count and workspace on the host before launch. Given only the buffer, it builds a short row as if it were a full one.

So the new argument states the longest live row in the batch. A serving stack that assembles the batch already has it -- it is `max(seqLens)`. No caller in aiter passes it yet, so nothing reaches the new kernel until a stack opts in. The tables below declare it.

- **It is a guarantee, not a hint.** Part of what it selects is compiled in, so a bound below the longest live row returns wrong indices rather than merely slower ones. It cannot be checked here without the sync this path exists to avoid. A bound above it is always correct; it only costs the win.
- **`None` declines the adaptive kernel and nothing else.** The chunked bands keep reading the physical width they were fitted on, so a call that passes nothing routes exactly where it routes today.
- **It never changes a result**, only which kernel produces it.

## Results

Every cell is scored, not only the ones the gate takes. A band takes a cell when the kernel is no slower than the best of the four and at least 1.05x faster than what runs there today; a smaller margin is noise. Every entry had to satisfy that on **both** slices below, so a cell that only clears it on the diagonal is not in the table. Nothing is behind on either slice.

A ratio is today's kernel over this PR's, so a declined cell is 1.00x by construction and the geomean covers every cell. Each card's own grid and per-cell winners are below.

Protocol: all four arms are timed the same way on every cell, under graph replay, and the cell's number is the median over its repeats; cells where the arms came out close were re-timed with more.

**On the diagonal**, where the buffer is exactly full.

| device | cells | cells taken | geomean | worst cell | behind |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI308X, gfx942, 80 CU | 1000 | 433 | 1.34x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300A, gfx942, 228 CU | 1000 | 388 | 1.35x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300X, gfx942, 304 CU | 1000 | 361 | 1.32x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI355X, gfx950, 256 CU | 1000 | 311 | 1.13x | 1.00x | 0 |

**On padded buffers**, a 1048576 buffer holding a shorter live row with `max_row_len` set to that length, which is what production allocates and what a serving stack would pass. Same table, looked up at the bound.

| device | cells | cells taken | geomean | worst cell | behind |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI308X, gfx942, 80 CU | 900 | 369 | 1.29x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300A, gfx942, 228 CU | 900 | 315 | 1.25x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300X, gfx942, 304 CU | 900 | 288 | 1.22x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI355X, gfx950, 256 CU | 900 | 238 | 1.10x | 1.00x | 0 |

All four entries are added by this PR. Cards not in these tables are untouched.

The bound is what makes the second table look like the first. Holding the live length fixed and widening the buffer to 1048576 should be free, and for the kernels that read `seq_lens` on the device it is; the adaptive kernel pays for it on the host unless it is told.
